opus-5.5.text:
The way I think about it is that the web was built for humans, and for twenty-five years search has been optimized for a human doing the clicking. You get ten blue links, you skim, you click, you go back, you reformulate. The ranking was tuned for that loop and for attention: what will a person click on.

Now the primary consumer of the web is increasingly going to be an AI agent. Agents use the web very differently. They don't need ten links ranked for clickability. They need the right tokens in their context window, the evidence that helps them reason and act. So the research problem, as I see it, is: what does the web look like when you design it from first principles for an AI as the user?

That breaks into a few hard pieces. One is retrieval quality measured differently. It isn't "did the top result get clicked," it's "did the agent end up with the correct, complete answer, and how efficiently did it get there." You're optimizing for accuracy per dollar and per unit of latency, not engagement. That changes what you index, how you chunk content, and what you return.

The second piece is the range of compute. Some questions are a quick lookup. Others are deep research: an agent might need to read hundreds of pages, cross-reference them, and verify claims. So we think of it as a spectrum where you can spend more compute to get a better answer, and you want that tradeoff to be explicit and controllable for the developer, almost like choosing a processor tier.

The third is verifiability. If agents are going to do real work, like due diligence, compliance, or filling out a spreadsheet of facts about thousands of companies, you need to know where every piece of information came from and how confident to be in it. Citations and calibrated confidence aren't nice-to-haves. They're core to the product.

And then there's a bigger, longer-term question underneath all of it: the economics of the open web. If agents read the web instead of humans, the old bargain where publishers get traffic and ads stops working. Part of the research problem, and honestly part of the mission, is figuring out an open, market-based web where the people creating content still have reason to keep creating it. If we just build better extraction without solving that, the web gets worse over time, and so do the agents relying on it.

So to me it's not just "build a better search engine." It's rethinking the interface between AI and the world's information, and making sure that interface is accurate, efficient, and sustainable.

r002.rationale: It says agents need the right tokens in their context window, but does not frame the task as selecting a thousand tokens from roughly a trillion web pages.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that web search was built for humans, and the whole system is tuned around human constraints. A person types a few words, scans ten blue links, clicks one or two, and the engine optimizes for that experience. Every design choice downstream of that, from how results are ranked to how much text is returned, assumes a human with limited patience on the other end.

An AI agent is a completely different consumer. It doesn't want ten links. It wants the actual evidence, the specific passages that answer the question, with enough context to reason over and enough provenance to trust. It can tolerate much more volume, it can issue many queries in parallel, and it cares far more about recall and precision on the facts than about a clean page layout. So the research problem, as we see it, is to rebuild the retrieval stack with the model as the user rather than the person.

That reframing changes a lot. It changes what you index, because you want the full content of a page, not a snippet. It changes how you rank, because the objective is "does this help the model produce a correct, grounded answer" rather than "will a person click this." And it changes the interface, because the input is often a rich, multi-part objective rather than a keyword string, and the output should be structured evidence rather than a list.

The hard part is evaluation. For human search you can look at clicks and dwell time. For agents, the right signal is whether the downstream task got done correctly, which means you have to build benchmarks around end-to-end accuracy on real research tasks and then work backward to figure out which retrieval decisions mattered. That loop, between the retrieval system and the model's actual performance, is where most of the interesting work lives for us.

r004.rationale: It says agents can issue parallel queries and tolerate more volume, but does not frame search compute as maximizing output quality within a compute or latency budget.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is: what does web search look like when the user is an AI rather than a human? A human can look at a page of results, click a few links, and decide what’s useful. An AI might be doing that as one step in a much longer task, so the information it needs—and the way you should deliver it—can be quite different.

That makes it more than a ranking problem. You have to understand what information the task requires, find the relevant sources, and return something the AI can reason over, with enough evidence to support its conclusions. And you have to decide when you’ve searched enough. Another search might resolve an uncertainty, or it might just add latency and cost.

The research question, then, is how to optimize that whole process. Can you give the AI the information it needs to do the downstream task well, within the time and compute budget available? That’s the lens I’d use, rather than looking only at whether an individual search result seems relevant.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding tasks and finding sources, but does not describe compressing model capabilities into tiny ranking models.

r002.rationale: It does not frame a query as selecting a thousand tokens from a corpus of roughly a trillion web pages.

r003.rationale: It does not mention organizing information across a memory hierarchy for fast access.

r004.rationale: It frames search as giving the AI what it needs to do the downstream task well within available time and compute, also noting latency and cost.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central research question is: what should web search look like when the consumer is an AI rather than a person? A lot of search today is designed to help someone find a page, click through, and read it. An AI system might need to gather evidence from many sources, reconcile conflicting information, and then use that information to complete a task.

That changes what you’re optimizing for. Finding a relevant page is one part of it, but you also care about whether the information is sufficient, whether it’s fresh, and whether the answer is supported by the sources. And you have to do that within some budget of time and computation.

So I think of it as a research problem around gathering evidence: given a task, what information should you look for, how should you look for it, and when do you have enough to proceed? Search becomes a component of reasoning, and the quality of that component affects what the entire system can accomplish.
